title: World models
caption:
Nobody filmed this. There's no game engine. The AI is imagining every frame as you move 🌍

World models are AI's next big race: Google's Genie 4, NVIDIA's Cosmos 3 and World Labs' Atlas all dropped in the last few weeks. Riya asks, Arjun explains:
1. Video model vs world model
2. The memory problem
3. Two ways to build a world
4. Why robots train inside dreams
5. Where it still breaks

Pause at the 2 quizzes and comment your guess 👇

Facts: Google DeepMind (Genie 3, Genie 4), TechCrunch (Oct 2026), NVIDIA Cosmos 3 blogs (Nov 2026), World Labs blog (Nov 2026).

Next up: AI shopping agents, just in time for Black Friday 🛒

scenes.title: WORLD MODELS
scenes.subtitle: AI that dreams worlds you can walk into

lines.vo: Arjun, look at this. Nobody filmed it? And there's no game engine?
lines.cap: Nobody FILMED this? No game ENGINE?

lines.vo: Nope. An A.I. is imagining every frame, live, as you move. It's called a world model.
lines.cap: AI imagines every FRAME as you move.

lines.vo: Isn't that just an A.I. video generator?
Close, but no. A video model makes a clip, and you watch it. A world model lets you act inside it.
lines.cap: Video: you WATCH. World: you ACT.

lines.vo: Press forward, turn left, and it responds. Like a game that nobody coded.
Here's the loop. You press a key.
lines.cap: The LOOP: you press a key.

lines.vo: The model predicts the very next frame, from everything so far, plus your action.
It shows that frame, then does it all again. For Genie 3, twenty four times a second.
lines.cap: Show it, REPEAT. 24 times a second.

lines.vo: So it's dreaming the game in real time.

scenes.label: QUIZ 1
scenes.question: Genie has no 3D engine inside. How does it draw the world?
options: It predicts the next frame, one at a time

lines.vo: Quiz time. Google's Genie has no 3D engine inside. So how does it draw the world?
lines.cap: QUIZ: no 3D engine. How does it DRAW?

lines.vo: Pause and guess. Three, two, one.
It predicts the next frame, one at a time. DeepMind calls it auto regressive. Each frame builds on the last one.
lines.cap: Next frame, ONE at a time.

lines.vo: Wait. If it only makes the next frame, what happens when I look away?
That's the hard part. You turn around, you turn back, and the tree has to still be there.
lines.cap: The tree has to STILL be there.

lines.vo: So the model has to remember what it drew. If it forgets, the world melts.
lines.cap: If it FORGETS, the world melts.

items.s: 720p, 24 fps, consistent for a few minutes

lines.vo: Google's Genie 3 runs at seven twenty p, twenty four frames a second, and stays consistent for a few minutes.
Its visual memory reaches back about a minute.
And the new one?
Genie 4 came out in late October. It adds sound, and you can type to change the world live. Make it rain, add a character. It's still a research preview.
lines.cap: Genie 4: SOUND + type to change it LIVE.

scenes.label: 3 · TWO WAYS TO BUILD A WORLD

lines.vo: Is everyone doing it this way?
lines.cap: Is EVERYONE doing it this way?

lines.vo: There are two camps. One dreams every frame live, like Genie. World Labs' Atlas can do that too, streaming up to fifteen frames a second from cloud G.P.U.s.
The other builds a real 3D scene. Atlas Viewfinder rebuilds a place from photos, and you can take it into tools like Blender.
So one is a dream, and the other is a set you can keep.
lines.cap: A DREAM vs a SET you keep.

lines.vo: Who actually needs this? Gamers?
Robots, mostly. In early November, NVIDIA released Cosmos 3, open world models for robots and cars.
One takes a robot arm's actions and predicts what the camera sees next. Another runs driving tests in a loop.
lines.cap: Arm ACTIONS in, next FRAMES out.

lines.vo: So the robot practises in a dream first.

scenes.label: QUIZ 2
scenes.question: Why train a robot inside a dream world?
options: Cheap, safe, and rare cases on repeat

lines.vo: Second quiz. Why train a robot inside a dream world, instead of the real one?
lines.cap: QUIZ 2: why train in a DREAM?

lines.vo: Pause and guess. Three, two, one.
It's cheap and safe. A robot can fail a thousand times, and you can replay rare moments, like a ball rolling into the road.
Okay. What's the catch?
Details drift the longer it runs. And text usually comes out messy, unless it was in your prompt.
It can't copy real places perfectly. And it runs on powerful cloud G.P.U.s, so it isn't cheap.
So. You act, it predicts the next frame, memory is the hard part, and robots train inside these dreams.
Exactly. Next up, A.I. shopping agents, just in time for Black Friday. Follow so you don't miss it.
